backups.overview: Little Big Chief Mountain (7,225 ft) sits on the King–Kittitas county line immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, just over half a mile from its taller neighbor Summit Chief Mountain (7,464 ft), with which it shares a long crest running toward Chimney Rock and Middle Chief along the Cascade divide about 10 miles northeast of Snoqualmie Pass. Fred Beckey, Wayne Swift, Joe Barto, and Campbell Brooks made the first ascent in August 1939; the peak's name honors Lorenz A. Nelson, a Mountaineers climber active on early first ascents of Mount Olympus, Mount Meany, and Chiwawa Mountain. It is a quieter, seldom-visited summit — every approach requires 10+ miles of wilderness trail plus cross-country travel, so it sees far fewer parties than the trailheads that access it.
backups.beta: This is a rarely climbed, route-finding-intensive scramble rather than a well-trodden trail. A 2014 party (Jim Brisbine) climbing from a camp at Williams Lake found the crux to be a wildly exposed notch on the northeast ridge, then Class 4-5 moves on a steep southwest face near the true summit; the party descended the 'easier' Class 3 east face but still ran into cliff bands that forced a traverse back onto the ascent line. A separate account similarly describes exposed Class 3 moves on the east face and a short Class 3 section gaining the north ridge, and a short rock notch is noted that some parties rate as low fifth class.
backups.turnaround: Given the long, remote approach and the North Cascades' typical afternoon-thunderstorm and weather-change risk in summer, set a firm turnaround time before starting the final ridge/notch scramble so the exposed sections and descent are not attempted in the dark or in deteriorating weather.
backups.rappels: 1-2 raps off the descent ridge (rope length not specified by source)
backups.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass to park at most trailheads.
backups.comms: No reliable cell service in the Middle Fork valley or on the peak; carry a satellite messenger.
backups.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

waypoints.name: Salmon La Sac Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee required; free self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk before entering Alpine Lakes Wilderness.
waypoints.directions: Drive Salmon La Sac Road (FR-4330) about 19 miles north from Cle Elum to its end, where the trailhead sits at roughly 2,500 feet. You need a Northwest Forest Pass or the day-use fee, and there is a kiosk for the free self-issue wilderness permit; fill one out before you enter the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. The road and trailhead are typically not fully clear until early to mid June, and the climb is best July through September.

waypoints.name: Alpine Lakes Wilderness Boundary
waypoints.note: Trail crosses the wilderness boundary sign on the gently undulating Waptus River Trail #1310; no motorized/mechanized travel beyond this point.
waypoints.directions: Head east from the parking area on the Waptus River Trail #1310. The first mile rolls over a couple of low forested rises before the grade settles; the wilderness boundary sign comes up shortly after that.

waypoints.name: Hour Creek Camp
waypoints.note: Bridgeless crossing of Hour Creek with an established campsite next to a small waterfall; ford can run high in early season.
waypoints.directions: The trail settles into a long, gentle grade alongside the Waptus River, crossing a string of small feeder creeks — water is reliable this whole stretch — and passing boggy meadow sections and old burn patches. Hour Creek itself has no bridge: an easy step across in normal summer flow, but pushy and cold during snowmelt.

waypoints.name: Waptus Pass Trail Junction (via Trail Creek Trail jct. at 6.9 mi)
waypoints.note: Trail leaves the Waptus River near the Trail Creek Trail #1322 junction (6.9 mi) and climbs about two miles to this junction with Waptus Pass Trail #1329 before dropping back toward Waptus Lake.
waypoints.directions: Continue up-river past the Trail Creek Trail #1322 junction near mile 6.9, then climb roughly two miles and about 1,100 ft away from the river to this junction. Stay on the Waptus River Trail rather than forking north toward Spade Lake.

waypoints.name: Waptus Lake / Chief Creek Ford
waypoints.note: Ford Chief Creek near the head of Waptus Lake (easy but wet, ~knee deep); established camps sit on either side of the crossing and serve as the jump-off for the peak.
waypoints.directions: The trail drops back toward the lake. The hiker bridge over the Waptus River below the lake washed out in 2007 and was never replaced, so take the horse-ford bypass and wade — a wide but shallow crossing in normal summer flow, and a serious proposition during snowmelt. Follow the lake's southeast shore, which holds steep snowfields into early summer and can warrant an ice axe, then ford Chief Creek near the head of the lake.

waypoints.name: Talus Basin Below the Summit Chief Group
waypoints.note: Leave the trail here and pick a way up through timber into the open talus basins below Little Big Chief's west side; route-finding through mounded talus is slow going.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail at the ford and work up through timber on no tread, aiming for the open ground below the peak's west side. It is roughly 2,500 ft of gain, and the mounded talus above the trees is slow, ankle-turning walking — allow far more time than the mileage suggests.

waypoints.name: Exposed Summit Notch
waypoints.note: Low fifth-class move through a narrow rock notch just below the summit ridge with significant exposure — the technical crux of the west-side scramble.

waypoints.name: Little Big Chief Mountain Summit
waypoints.note: True summit on the King/Kittitas county line just southwest of Dutch Miller Gap; sweeping views of Summit Chief, Waptus Lake, and Bears Breast.

backups.detailed_rack: A light alpine kit rather than a full rack: a 30-60m rope for the short belayed step(s) and any rappel, a few slings for tree or rock anchors, and a helmet. An ice axe is recommended if snow lingers in the approach basin or on the shaded ridge.
pro_tips: Combine with Summit Chief area peaks
Plan as a multi-day trip
watch_out: Cross-country travel above Chief Creek (talus, heather, occasional snowfields) has no maintained tread — route-finding to the correct gully and ridge breach near 7,100 ft is easy to get wrong in poor visibility.
The final summit block is guarded by an exposed notch/step reported as low class 5 on other documented lines up this peak; know your party's comfort soloing exposed rock before committing.
The Waptus River ford can be dangerous in high or early-season flow — cross in the morning before snowmelt peaks, and be willing to turn back.
backups.pro_needs: Minimal protection needed — natural rock and tree anchors with slings are sufficient for the short technical notch; no fixed gear or pitons are reported on this line.
backups.approach: From the Salmon La Sac Trailhead (end of Salmon La Sac Rd/FR-4330, ~19 mi north of Cle Elum), pick up the Waptus River Trail #1310 heading east into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. The first mile or so rolls over a couple of low forested hills before the trail settles into a long, gentle grade alongside the Waptus River, crossing numerous small feeder creeks (reliable water the whole way) and skirting boggy meadow sections and old burn patches. Around mile 7-8 stay on the Waptus River Trail (rather than forking north toward Spade Lake) and continue to the Waptus River crossing below Waptus Lake — the old hiker bridge here washed out in 2007 and was never replaced, so expect a genuine ford, roughly knee-deep in normal summer flow and more serious during snowmelt. From the outlet, the trail follows the lake's southeast shore, a stretch that holds steep snowfields well into early summer and can warrant an ice axe. Beyond Waptus Lake, continue on toward Lake Ivanhoe and the Chief Creek drainage; most parties camp near the Chief Creek ford, roughly 12-13 miles in, which puts the bulk of the mileage behind you before the actual climb. A commonly cited variation leaves the main trail about 1/3 mile south of Lake Ivanhoe and follows the creek draining into the Waptus River from that point, gaining the west side of the peak more directly. From the Chief Creek crossing, faint but generally trackable switchbacks climb the open slopes toward Little Big Chief's west ridge/west face — figure on 4,000+ ft of additional elevation gain above the ford to the summit, a full day's effort in its own right. As trees thin out the route becomes cross-country travel over heather benches and talus, with loose scree and route-finding (rather than any single obstacle) as the main hazards; the final few hundred feet narrow onto an exposed summit ridge with class 3-4 scrambling through a notch just below the top.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: back down through the exposed summit notch onto the west ridge/west face slopes, then down to the Chief Creek drainage and the Waptus River Trail for the long walk out. The notch just below the summit is the one real technical spot. Many parties simply downclimb it (class 3-4, exposed but with positive holds); others choose to protect it with a single short rappel — roughly 30-50 ft — off a sling/cordelette around a chockstone or horn. No bolted or fixed anchors are reported anywhere on this peak (the rock throughout the Little Big Chief massif is consistently loose/choss), so plan to build and retrieve a natural anchor; a single 30m rope is more than enough for this one rappel. This matches the pattern on the mountain's other aspects — parties on the north ridge and on the Falcon/Northwest Face route both report a single short rappel or two off natural anchors right at the summit block — so a short, single-rappel (or downclimb-only) exit is the reasonable expectation here too. Below the notch, retrace the talus/heather slopes back to the Chief Creek ford, re-cross the Waptus River below the lake, and reverse the Waptus River Trail back to Salmon La Sac; this is a long enough approach/descent that most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with a base camp near Chief Creek or Lake Ivanhoe rather than a car-to-car push.
backups.bail: There is no established rappel/walk-off bail line reported for this route; retreat means reversing the ridge and notch section back onto the east-slope descent line. Turn around before committing to the exposed notch if conditions, party ability, or time are marginal.

approach_variants.name: Waptus River Trail from Salmon La Sac
approach_variants.notes: The southern approach, and a long one — most parties treat it as a two- or three-day trip rather than a push. From the Salmon La Sac road end, take the Waptus River trail east into the wilderness. The first mile rolls over low forested hills before the trail settles into a long gentle grade beside the river, crossing many small feeder creeks — water is reliable the whole way — and skirting boggy meadow and old burn. Around the seven-to-eight mile mark stay on the Waptus River trail rather than forking north toward Spade Lake. The river crossing below Waptus Lake is a genuine FORD: the old hiker bridge washed out and was never replaced, so expect knee-deep water in normal summer flow. Past the outlet the trail runs the lake's southeast shore, a stretch that holds steep snow into early summer. Continue toward Lake Ivanhoe and the Chief Creek drainage; most parties camp near the Chief Creek ford.
approach_variants.season: July to September. The lakeshore stretch holds steep snowfields into early summer and the river ford is far more serious during snowmelt.
hazards: Unbridged Waptus River ford near the lake — cold, swift, and far more serious in snowmelt
Steep snowfields on the lake's southeast shore into early summer
Loose scree and route-finding, rather than any single obstacle, as the main hazard on the upper slopes
Exposed low-fifth-class notch below the summit ridge that some parties rope
Loose rock throughout — no fixed or bolted anchors are reported anywhere on this peak
approach_variants.baseFinding: From the Chief Creek crossing, faint switchbacks climb open slopes toward the peak's west ridge. The base of the climbing proper is where the TREES STOP: below the treeline you are on a trackable, if faint, boot line, and above it there is no tread at all, only continuous heather benches and talus with loose scree — that transition is the start, and there is no cairn, anchor or marker at it. The confirming feature comes much higher and is the one technical spot on the route: the final few hundred feet narrow onto an exposed summit ridge with a NARROW ROCK NOTCH just below the top, and if your line never reaches a notch you have drifted off it. Negative markers: if you are on maintained tread, you have not left the Waptus River trail yet; if you find yourself on the far side of the mountain looking down a valley toward a steel bridge on a river trail, you have crossed the divide into the Middle Fork drainage and are above the routes approached from the north.

approach_variants.name: Direct creek line below Lake Ivanhoe
approach_variants.notes: A commonly cited variation that shortens the upper approach. Rather than continuing all the way to the Chief Creek camp, leave the main trail a short distance south of Lake Ivanhoe and follow the creek that drains from there into the Waptus River, gaining the peak's west side more directly. Everything below that point is identical to the standard approach, including the river ford.
hazards: No path at all above the trail; the creek is the only handrail
Loose scree and brush on the lower slopes
Same unbridged Waptus ford and snow-holding lakeshore as the standard approach
Exposed notch below the summit ridge
approach_variants.baseFinding: Leave the trail where the creek draining toward the Waptus meets it, a short distance south of Lake Ivanhoe, and use the creek as your handrail — the creek line IS the route-finding, because there is no path. The base of the climbing is again the point where the timber thins out and the ground becomes unbroken heather bench and talus running up toward the west ridge crest. The check that you are on the right drainage is that it leads you up onto the WEST side of the peak, with the summit ridge above and to your right as you climb. Negative marker: if the creek is taking you away from the peak rather than under it, or you find yourself dropping toward a lake, you are on the wrong drainage — this line gains ground continuously from the moment you leave the trail.

As trees thin out it becomes cross-country travel over heather benches and talus, with loose scree and route-finding (rather than any single obstacle) as the main hazards.

bivy.name: Talus Basin Below the Summit Chief Group
Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
bivy.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.
bivy.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
bivy.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.

backups.overview: The peak's original 1939 first-ascent line and its easiest way up: heather, talus and snowfield travel along the northeast ridge to a cirque below the east face, finished by one or two short belayed pitches of 3rd-4th class (occasionally low 5th) rock to the summit.
backups.beta: Approached via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail to Dutch Miller Gap, the route climbs about 500 feet of heather and rock steps up the northeast ridge to an open bench, then crosses a snowfield into a cirque below the east face. Two short (roughly 60-foot) belayed pitches of 3rd-4th class rock lead to the summit area; at the top of the first pitch, move climber's left to find the direct finishing pitch. Reported variations include the north ridge from the upper snowfield, or four pitches of roped class-4 slabs taken directly. A separate approach from Pete Lake/Summit Chief camp reaches Little Big Chief's northeast basin and a ridge notch guarded by a low-5th-class crux (a large vertical crack) that most parties rope up for.
backups.turnaround: The descent retraces exposed ridge and snow terrain, so turn around with enough daylight to be off the summit snowfield and ridge before dark. Allow for slower travel in poor visibility or soft/refrozen snow, and for the long approach back to the trailhead.
backups.rock_grade: 3rd-4th class (a low-5th-class crux on the alternate northeast-basin approach)
backups.rappels: No fixed rappel stations; slings for tree or rock anchors cover any rappels on the short belayed pitches.
backups.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. No recreation pass is required at the Dingford Creek Trailhead.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage around Dutch Miller Gap, in the Summit Chief Valley, or on the Necklace Valley approach — this is deep backcountry in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Carry a satellite communicator.
backups.descent: Reverse the route: downclimb or rappel the short roped pitches into the east-face cirque, then descend the snowfield and the heather and rock steps of the northeast ridge toward Dutch Miller Gap — or, via the alternate approach, back into the northeast basin.

loose rock on heather benches, rock steps and the ridge
exposed notch on the ridge, minimum 5th class and vertical to overhanging on its north side
small, precarious summit requiring careful downclimbing

The Pete Lake approach lets you combine Little Big Chief with Summit Chief Mountain in one trip
Carry a rope even though most of the route is scrambling — the ridge-notch crux and any moats are more comfortably protected with one
watch_out: A separate account of this side of the peak describes a wildly exposed, near-vertical Class 4 notch on the northeast ridge as the crux
Descending via an unplanned northeast-trending couloir has cliffed a party out well above the valley floor — stick to the known line
Snowfield conditions vary widely by season and year and can require an ice axe or crampons
Route-finding in the basin below the east face is fuzzy in published descriptions — GPS tracks are recommended
A wasp nest has been reported along the Pete Lake approach basin
backups.pro_needs: Minimal formal protection: the two roped pitches are typically belayed off natural features (trees, horns) rather than placed gear, so slings and cord for anchors suffice. An ice axe is useful while snow lingers in the cirque.
backups.best_season: Climbable roughly June through September; a mid-June ascent has been documented (party carried a rope for the low-5th crux and moat crossings), while July-September is generally recommended once snowfields have consolidated and seasonal hazards (loose rock, wasps in the basin) are reduced.
backups.approach: From the Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead, follow Dutch Miller Gap Trail 1030 up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie valley about 14-15 miles to Dutch Miller Gap, passing Hardscrabble Horse Camp and the Williams Lake trail junction along the way. Little Big Chief sits immediately southwest of the gap, reached from the gap itself by an off-trail scramble up the peak's east slope/northeast ridge, with a short but exposed class 4 notch as the crux below the summit. An alternate, longer approach comes from the east via the Necklace Valley Trail off Foss River Road (Skykomish/US 2 side), crossing La Bohn Gap before dropping to Dutch Miller Gap. For this specific route: continue the standard Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail all the way up to Dutch Miller Gap, then climb directly above the gap onto the peak's northeast ridge/face — no cross-country detour into Summit Chief Valley needed.
backups.descent_text: From the summit, reverse the two short belayed pitches — using tree or sling anchors for any rappels — back into the cirque below the east face. Cross the snowfield and descend the roughly 500 feet of heather and rock steps on the northeast ridge toward Dutch Miller Gap. Parties who approached via Pete Lake/Summit Chief instead downclimb the ridge-notch crux (often roped) and drop into the northeast basin to regain camp. Do not improvise a shortcut gully: a first-hand account of this east-side face descended the East Face at class 3 but became cliffed out about 600 ft above the valley floor after straying into a northeast-trending couloir.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward. The roped sections are short (roughly 60 ft each) and can be downclimbed or rappelled from tree and sling anchors — rappel rather than downclimb the final belayed step. Below that the route is walk-off heather and snow, the exception being active snowfall or whiteout on the upper snowfield.

pitch_detail.notes: Heather and rock steps up the NE ridge (~500 ft) to an open snow bench.
Ascend through the cirque below the east face and up the summit snowfield.
Final ~60-ft belayed pitch direct to the summit, or move left for the alternate direct-summit variant.

backups.itinerary: Usually a 2-3 day trip and often combined with a neighbouring peak (Summit Chief or Overcoat) from a backcountry camp near Dutch Miller Gap or Summit Chief Lake: approach and camp on day 1, climb the northeast ridge/face and return to camp on day 2, hike out on day 3. Strong parties climb it as a long day from a camp already at the gap.

approach_variants.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie to Dutch Miller Gap
approach_variants.notes: The standard way. From the Middle Fork Snoqualmie road end, follow the Dutch Miller Gap trail up the valley for a long day — roughly fourteen to fifteen miles — passing the horse camp and the Williams Lake trail junction on the way to the gap. Most parties break this over two days and camp near Williams Lake or at the gap. There is no cross-country detour for this route: stay on the trail to the top.
approach_variants.season: July to September; recorded ascents cluster in August and September. The upper cirque holds snow well into summer, so carry an axe.
hazards: Snow lingering in the approach cirque well into summer, with variable soft, icy or moat-riddled conditions
Loose rock on the heather and rock steps, on the ridge and on the face
No cell coverage, and a remote position that makes rescue difficult
The gap is a trail high point with several ways off it — confirm you are on the southwest side before committing
approach_variants.baseFinding: The climbing starts DIRECTLY ABOVE THE GAP. From the low point of Dutch Miller Gap, turn onto the peak immediately southwest of it — the first ground above the trail that needs hands is the start, roughly five hundred feet of heather and rock steps rising onto the northeast ridge. The physical test is the sequence: heather steps give way to an OPEN BENCH, and above the bench you cross a SNOWFIELD into a cirque below the east face; if you have not crossed snow you have not reached the cirque, and the two short belayed pitches to the summit start from it. At the top of the first of those pitches, move climber's LEFT for the direct finish. Negative markers: if you left the trail at a small steel bridge well below the gap and dropped south into a side valley, you are heading for the long gully-and-crack route on the far side of the mountain; if you are looking up nine hundred feet of talus at a prominent left-trending gully, you are under that route and not this one.

approach_variants.name: Necklace Valley and La Bohn Gap from the north
approach_variants.notes: A longer alternative from the other side of the divide: the Necklace Valley trail off the Foss River road, over La Bohn Gap, then down to Dutch Miller Gap. It joins the standard line at the gap, so everything above is identical. Worth knowing about mainly as a through-trip option or if the Middle Fork road end is not usable.
hazards: Long approach over a second pass, with snow on La Bohn Gap into summer
Loose rock above the gap
Remote, rescue-difficult terrain with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: You are aiming for the same point as the standard approach: the low saddle of Dutch Miller Gap, with the peak on its southwest side. Coming from the north you drop TO the gap rather than climbing to it, so the check is that you have finished descending and the peak is now above you on the left. The climbing begins at the first hands-on heather-and-rock steps above the gap, leading to an open bench and then a snowfield crossing into the cirque below the east face. Negative marker: if you are still descending and the ground ahead keeps dropping into a valley, you have passed the gap and are heading down the Middle Fork.

approach_variants.name: Pete Lake and Summit Chief camp from the east
approach_variants.notes: The eastern option, from a camp near Pete Lake and Summit Chief. It does not reach Dutch Miller Gap at all — it comes at the peak's northeast basin from the other side and joins the route higher up. It is the approach that puts the ridge notch in your path, which the trail-to-the-gap line avoids.
hazards: Exposed low-fifth-class crux move at the ridge notch, which most parties belay
Route-finding through the northeast basin's cliff bands
Loose rock throughout
Remote with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding: From camp, work into the peak's NORTHEAST BASIN. The route is guarded by a RIDGE NOTCH, and the notch is identified by a single feature: a LARGE VERTICAL CRACK forming a low-fifth-class step that most parties rope up for. If the notch you have reached can be walked through, it is not this one. Above the notch the ground eases and joins the snowfield and cirque used by the trail approach. Negative marker: if you are standing in a broad trail saddle with tread underfoot, you are at Dutch Miller Gap and on the standard line, where no such crack step exists.

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
bivy.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.
bivy.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
bivy.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included

backups.overview: Buck Mountain (8,534 ft) is the high point of the peaks ringing Buck Creek Pass in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, named for pioneer USFS surveyor Albert H. Sylvester. Its north and east faces are composed of dark, almost black schist that gives the summit a brooding look above the pass; the summit affords sweeping views of Glacier Peak (about 9 miles west), Clark Mountain (its taller parent peak, ~4 miles southwest), Liberty Cap, and Helmet Butte. First climbed in 1948 by Carl Suback and Ray Rigg, the peak is now one of the most popular scrambles in the area — typically climbed as a side trip from a multi-day backpack based at Buck Creek Pass, and rated as an Alpine Scramble.
backups.beta: The usual way up comes from the west, which means a long way round even though the peak stands only about three miles from Trinity. From the Trinity Trailhead, the Buck Creek Trail (#1513) climbs about 9.6 miles and 3,100 ft to Buck Creek Pass. From the pass an unmaintained high route winds around the west side of Liberty Cap and south to High Pass; contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, climb a short Class 3 step onto the ridge just south of Point 7839, and walk down into Louis Creek Basin to camp. From the basin, broad pumice, talus and low-angle snow lead up the south and southwest slopes to the crest, and loose, slabby schist with one short Class 3-4 step near a horn goes to the summit. Some parties come in over Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa valley instead. A direct line from King Lake on the east side exists but is brushy, involves a river ford, and is seldom used.
backups.turnaround: Set a firm turnaround time before starting the summit push from camp and honor it — afternoon thunderstorms, the long remote approach, and loose schist on the exposed Class 3 terrain make a late or rushed descent significantly more hazardous.

backups.pro_needs: This is an unroped Class 2-3 scramble with no fixed protection or established rappel anchors; parties uncomfortable with the exposed schist moves near the summit sometimes carry a rope and a few slings for a hip-belay or short rappel, but it is not standard gear for this line.
backups.approach: From the Trinity Trailhead (Glacier Peak Wilderness, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk) at the end of the Chiwawa River Road/FR-6200 (~2,800 ft), follow Buck Creek Trail #1513. The trail splits from the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 within the first mile and climbs steadily through forest; around mile 2.75-3 it crosses the upper Chiwawa River on a footbridge that is weathered/damaged, so treat it with care in high runoff and have a wading backup plan in early season. Above the crossing the trail is a long, fairly shadeless, grinding ascent (mosquitoes/black flies are heavy in July) through forest and then subalpine meadow along the flank of Middle Ridge, opening into increasingly good wildflower and Glacier Peak views as you climb. At roughly 9.25-10 miles and about 3,000-3,300 ft of gain, the trail tops out at Buck Creek Pass (~5,800-5,900 ft) - one of the most scenic passes in the Cascades, with a reliable spring near the pass for water (last dependable source before the basin). Beyond the pass there is no maintained trail: pick up the well-used climbers'/boot path that switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap and the High Pass Trail junction, then leave that path to contour and traverse west/southwest, staying below Liberty Cap, into the upper basin below Buck Mountain's south and west aspects (Louis Creek Basin, ~6,700 ft) - the standard camp for a two-day trip. Follow the ridge crest through Class 2-3 terrain (stepping to locally 3-4 near a horn/gendarme close to the true summit) on loose, rubbly, slabby schist to the top; the summit crest has several bumps within feet of each other, so take care identifying the true high point. Primary approach hazards: rockfall/loose schist (helmet recommended, especially with parties above or below), the river crossing in high water, no reliable water source between the pass and the basin in a dry year, and route-finding above Buck Creek Pass since the climbers' path is intermittent. An alternate historic approach reaches Buck Mountain via Little Giant Pass and the Napeequa Valley, used for longer traverses.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb - no rappelling is involved on the standard South Ridge route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 2-3 (locally 3-4 near the summit horn) loose, rubbly schist back down the ridge crest to the low-angle snowfield/basin around 7,400 ft, then descend the pumice and talus slopes back to the Louis Creek Basin camp (~6,700 ft). From there, traverse back east below Liberty Cap to rejoin the boot path down to Buck Creek Pass, and finish on the maintained Buck Creek Trail #1513 for the roughly 9.25-10 mile, ~3,000-3,300 ft descent back to the Trinity Trailhead. Trip reports on this route put summit-day round trip from a Buck Creek Pass/Louis Creek Basin camp at roughly 4 hours; given a car-to-car round trip of roughly 30 miles, most parties treat this as an overnight (camp at Buck Creek Pass or the upper basin) rather than a single push, though strong parties have done it in a long day. The main descent hazard is the same loose schist encountered on the way up - downclimbing loose rock is generally more dangerous than ascending it, so descend deliberately, test holds, and keep the group tight (or move one at a time) through the Class 3-4 band near the summit to avoid kicking rock onto climbers below. Rappels: 0.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward on this unroped scramble: descend the same slopes to Louis Creek Basin and reverse the high route to Buck Creek Pass. No technical or rope descent is needed on the standard line, but the high route itself is long and dry, so a retreat from the basin is still a full day out.

days.note: From the Trinity trailhead (2,800 ft) at the end of Chiwawa River Road, hike the Buck Creek Trail (No. 1513) about 9.6 miles and 3,100 ft to Buck Creek Pass, and fill up with water there. Follow the old High Pass trail around the west side of Liberty Cap and south to High Pass, where the tread fades into talus and snow, then contour through the pass and under Mount Berge and climb a short Class 3 step onto the ridge just south of Point 7839. An easy walk-off drops into Louis Creek Basin to camp. A long, dry, exposed day once past the pass.

climate.typical: East-slope Cascades transitional climate: Pacific storm systems drop heavy, wet snow on the approach through winter and spring via orographic lift as they hit the peaks, while summers are drier and more settled than the west side of the range; afternoon thunderstorms are possible in late summer.

bySeason.spring: Deep, avalanche-prone snowpack on the approach slopes and summit gullies
bySeason.summer: Best window, generally dry rock from mid/late July through September, but watch for afternoon thunderstorms
bySeason.winter: Full snow cover; road access to Trinity Trailhead typically closed by snow even in normal years

emergency.notes: Remote wilderness terrain with no cell coverage past the trailhead; a satellite communicator is strongly advised. All 911 calls in Chelan County route through RiverCom dispatch; the Chelan County Sheriff's Office Search & Rescue unit is the primary responder for the area. Note the active 2026 Chiwawa River Road closure adds significant time/distance to any self-rescue or evacuation.

approach_variants.name: Trinity to Buck Creek Pass, then the High Pass high route around the west side
approach_variants.notes:
Start at Trinity at the end of the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, at about 2,800 ft. Take the Buck Creek trail #1513, which splits off the Chiwawa River trail within the first mile and climbs steadily to Buck Creek Pass — roughly six hours and about 3,100 ft of gain.

Why this way round at all is worth understanding before you commit: Buck sits only about three miles from Trinity as the crow flies and is Class 2-3 from the south-west, but a long rugged ridge runs north and south of it and there is no road or trail up the Napeequa on the west, so the normal route is a very long way round. The two documented ways to reach that west side are the high route north from Buck Creek Pass and Little Giant Pass from the south.

At the pass there is a large established camp with toilets just before the switchbacks up toward Liberty Cap. FILL UP WITH WATER THERE — there is none for the next four miles and the ridge walk is fully sun-exposed.

Follow the old High Pass trail as it winds high around the side of Liberty Cap, then south for several miles until the tread dies out in talus and hard snowfields at High Pass; crampons are worth having for that. Contour through the pass and under Mount Berge, then angle up to the ridge crest just south of Point 7839. A short section of Class 3 reaches a faint saddle from which there is an easy walk-off down into Louis Creek Basin.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the traverse from the Berge saddle crosses steep heather that is nasty when wet, and holds snow into summer
hazards: No water for four miles beyond Buck Creek Pass on an exposed ridge
Steep heather ledges at the Berge saddle, very sketchy when wet
Waterfall slabs below the traverse line if you lose too much height
Hard snowfields at High Pass wanting crampons
Loose rubbly schist on the summit crest, with a fatal fall on record on this peak
Burn scar on the lower Buck Creek trail — hot, and blowdown
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The critical instruction on the traverse is about HEIGHT, and it comes with a stated consequence: from the saddle south of Berge, curving right around the bowl toward the mountain, STAY HIGH. Drop too low and you end up in steep waterfall slabs. If you are looking at running water over slabby ground, you have lost too much elevation and should climb back.

The arrival is unmistakable and it is not rock: you reach a beautiful forested bench with larches — good enough that parties note it as a campsite — and CROSS A RIVER. Once across that river you are at the base of Buck.

Above there the ground is broad pumice, talus and low-angle snowfield up to the south ridge around 7,400 ft, and then rubbly slabby schist along the crest with a short step up to Class 3-4 near a horn close to the top.

SUMMIT WARNING, and it is a genuine unresolved disagreement rather than a caution: parties do not agree how many summits Buck has or which is highest. One party climbed the middle of the long crest, found the register there, and judged it higher than both the north point and the south by twenty feet or more. Another says the south is the true one. A third found the register — dated 1967 — on the NORTH horn and reported the two tops as roughly equal. Only one of those parties actually measured anything. The summit crest holds several bumps within a few feet of each other, so expect to walk the crest rather than to arrive at an obvious high point, and do not treat a register as proof.

A useful sighting cue from a party approaching by a different line: the summit does not come into view until you reach the flat ground around 8,000 ft, in an upper cirque one climber described as looking like the flying bridge of a boat.

This mountain has killed someone — a climber fell fifty feet scrambling on a route on the east side, direct from Trinity, in 2018. The direct east line involves a river ford and a savage brushy bushwhack and is generally recommended as a descent rather than an ascent.

climbing_route.label: Pumice and talus slopes to the south ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the basin, ascend broad pumice and talus slopes and a low-angle snowfield to gain the south ridge around 7,400 ft; an ice axe, and crampons in early season, are worth carrying.

climbing_route.label: South ridge crest to the summit
climbing_route.notes: Follow the ridge crest through Class 2-3 terrain, stepping to locally 3-4 near a horn/gendarme close to the true summit, on loose, rubbly, slabby schist. Rockfall/loose schist is the main hazard - helmet recommended, especially with parties above or below. The summit crest has several bumps within feet of each other, so take care identifying the true high point.

bivy.name: Buck Creek Pass and the High Pass camps
bivy.notes: Buck Creek Pass at about 5,800 feet is the base for three peaks in this zone that have nothing to do with Glacier Peak's own approaches. Helmet Butte sits half a mile northeast of the pass and is the shortest objective from here. Buck Mountain rises directly south across the valley and is normally taken by leaving the Buck Creek trail lower down for the east ridge of Cleator and the Buck–Berge col, which also gives Mount Berge. From the pass a way trail continues north over Flower Dome to High Pass, which is both a fine high camp in its own right and the link over into the Napeequa, tying this side of the zone to Clark and Luahna. Getting here is around ten miles and three thousand feet of steady forest walking up Buck Creek from Trinity, so it is a full first day. It is a scenic and genuinely popular pass, which for a climbing party means arriving early enough to get a site. When the Chiwawa road is shut at Atkinson Flat the trailhead itself is roughly eleven road miles further on, which turns a two-day trip into a four-day one or a long bike shuttle.
bivy.water: A stream at the pass is the main supply and is reliable through the season; the higher camps toward High Pass run on snowmelt only and can be dry by September
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the Trinity trailhead, twelve-person party limit, Northwest Forest Pass for parking. Fires are prohibited where posted and the meadow ground here is exactly the kind of place that gets posted — carry a stove. Camp on the bare established sites rather than in the heather. The road is the real permit question: the Chiwawa River road is closed from Atkinson Flat north to Trinity under a storm order running through the end of 2027, with no reopening estimate, and a large 2026 fire closure covered the same road on top of it.
bivy.capacity: Several established forested and meadow-edge sites at the pass itself, enough for a few parties, with rougher and more exposed ground higher toward Flower Dome and High Pass

backups.overview: Esmeralda Peaks form a rugged, multi-summit ridge at the south end of the Teanaway Range in the Wenatchee Mountains, straddling the boundary of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness about 2.5 miles south of Ingalls Peak. The massif has an east and a west summit roughly 10 vertical feet apart, with older topos disagreeing on which is the true high point — most parties tag both. It sits on the USGS Mount Stuart quadrangle and is a popular moderate scramble objective with close-up views of Mt. Stuart and, from the ridge, distant Mt. Rainier. The standard line described here comes from the De Roux Creek valley to the south: a valley trail to a house-sized boulder at its last switchback, then a sustained Class 2 scree and talus slope to the west summit.
backups.beta: From the De Roux trailhead (3,800 ft), follow the Boulder-De Roux Trail #1392 roughly 3 miles west up the valley between Esmeralda Peaks and Koppen Mountain, passing several waterfalls, to a scree field near the final switchback (~5,600 ft) marked by a house-sized boulder. Leave the trail here and climb straight up a sustained, ~1,100 ft Class 2 scree/talus slope to the west summit (6,765 ft, true high point and register location); many topo maps mark the eastern summit (~10 ft lower) as the true top, so most parties tag both. The upper 100-150 ft is loose broken rock but not technically difficult; no rope is normally needed.
backups.turnaround: Set a turnaround time that gets you off the summit ridge before typical July–August afternoon thunderstorms build over the Teanaway high country.
backups.rappels: None — Class 2 walk-off descent, no rappels required

backups.descent: Downclimb the same scree and talus slope to the house-sized boulder at the trail's last switchback, then walk out the Boulder-De Roux Trail. Keeping to the trees beside the boulder field on the way down avoids most of the loose talus.

what_to_bring: sun protection — the south-facing scree slope has little shade
pro_tips: Tag both the east and west summits — topos disagree on the true high point, and the summit register sits on the west summit
Note the house-sized boulder at the last switchback on the way up; it is your target on the way back down
Filter water along the valley trail — the scree slope and summits are dry

Loose, exposure-prone talus low on the ridge

backups.pro_needs: None; a rope/rack is not used on the standard route.
backups.approach: Start at the De Roux trailhead and campground (~3,800 ft), on the left about 8 miles up gravel FR-9737 beyond the end of the paved North Fork Teanaway Road. Take the Boulder-De Roux Trail #1392 west, crossing the North Fork Teanaway and then De Roux Creek on bridges. About a mile in, keep right where the De Roux spur branches left, on the trail signed for Gallagher Head Lake. The trail climbs steadily up the valley between Esmeralda Peaks and Koppen Mountain, crosses the creek again on rocks or logs (awkward in snowmelt), passes several waterfalls, and makes its last switchback across a talus ridge at roughly 5,500-5,600 ft, where a house-sized boulder sits beside the tread. Leave the trail there on the boulder's climber's left and head up the hillside on a northeast bearing. Above is about 1,100 ft of sustained Class 2 scree and talus with no marked path; the line beneath the southwest ridge and the talus farther to climber's right both go, and a boulder field farther west is an alternative if the direct slope is too loose. The top 100-150 ft is loose broken rock. The west summit is a walk-up and very slightly higher than the east summit, which is the one the maps mark; most parties tag both. The round trip is about 7 miles with roughly 3,100 ft of gain, and there is no water once you leave the valley trail.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappelling. Retrace the ascent line down the Class 2 scree and talus slope, aiming back for the trail's last switchback; staying in the trees beside the boulder field on the way down avoids most of the loose talus. Rejoin the Boulder-De Roux Trail at the house-sized boulder and follow it back down the valley to the De Roux trailhead. The east and west summits are close enough to link along the connecting ridge before descending. No fixed anchors or rope work are reported; the hazards are loose rock underfoot, rockfall onto parties below, and finding the right line back to the switchback in low cloud, since the open slopes look alike.
backups.bail: From anywhere on the slope, retreat the way you came to the trail's last switchback; from there it is maintained trail all the way back to the De Roux trailhead.

~1,100 ft of sustained, loose scree and talus up the southwest slope to the west (true high point, 6,765 ft) summit; upper 100-150 ft is loose broken rock.
Short ridge scramble between the west and east summits; the west holds the register, though many topo maps mark the east as the true summit.

approach_variants.name: Boulder-De Roux Trail #1392 to the last switchback
approach_variants.notes: This is the standard approach. From the De Roux trailhead follow the Boulder-De Roux Trail west up the valley between the peaks and the mountain opposite; at the junction a mile or so in, the left branch is the signed De Roux spur and the way on is the right-hand trail signed for Gallagher Head Lake. That climbs steadily for another mile and a half, topping out at a creek crossing that takes some balance, and passes several waterfalls before making its final switchback across a talus ridge below an open scree field. The Esmeralda Basin trail on the far side of the massif connects to this one only as a long loop by way of the jeep road and the lake, so it is a different way round to the same departure rather than a separate climbing line.
approach_variants.season: July into October. The slope faces south and clears early, though the scree is at its worst fully dry.
hazards: A sustained scree and talus slope of roughly 1,100 ft with nothing to hold a slip
Navigation through the meadows, tree cover and upper boulder fields is genuinely tricky and many paths lead up with none of them obvious
The upper hundred to hundred and fifty feet is loose broken rock, easy to send down onto a party below
One short section of steeper scrambling has been used to reach the final summit block

No water once you leave the valley trail
approach_variants.baseFinding: A HOUSE-SIZED BOULDER AT THE LAST SWITCHBACK IS THE MARKER, AND YOU LEAVE THE TRAIL ON ITS CLIMBER'S LEFT. Walking up the valley past the waterfalls, the trail makes its final switchback across a talus ridge somewhere around 5,500 to 5,600 ft, and a single boulder the size of a house sits at that turn. Leave the tread there, on the boulder's climber's-left side, and head straight up the hillside on a northeast bearing. The overshoot tell is unmistakable: past that last switchback the trail stops climbing altogether and begins a long traverse toward the lake at the head of the valley, so if you are contouring rather than gaining and no big rock has appeared, you have gone by it. The upper mountain comes into view around 6,200 ft. Nothing above is marked and many faint paths lead up — none is the route, and either the line under the southwest ridge or the talus further climber's right will go. At the top there are two knobs a couple of hundred yards apart: the western one is a walk-up and is very slightly the higher, while the eastern is the one the maps mark. Tag both.

climbing_route.label: Scree and talus above the house-sized boulder
climbing_route.notes: Leave the trail at the boulder on the last switchback (~5,500-5,600 ft), on its climber's left, and climb northeast up about 1,100 ft of sustained, loose scree and talus. No path is marked and many faint ones lead up; the line under the southwest ridge and the talus farther to climber's right both go, and a boulder field farther west is an alternative when the direct slope is too loose. Lingering snow early in the season may call for an axe.

climbing_route.label: Upper slope and the two summits
climbing_route.notes: The upper 100-150 ft is loose broken rock. The western knob is a walk-up and very slightly higher; the eastern one, a couple of hundred yards away, is the one marked on maps. Tag both.

bivy.name: Lake Ann bench and the upper Esmeralda Basin camps
bivy.notes: The Esmeralda-side camp that is not Headlight Basin, and the one that actually serves the two peaks at the head of this valley. Esmeralda Peaks are scrambled directly from the basin on their standard route, and Fortune Peak's standard line goes up the basin and over the pass near Lake Ann before turning up the peak; both are honest day trips from the road end, so this is a place to sleep when the party is slow, the day is short, or you want two summits without driving twice. The trail leaves the road end at about 4,500 feet and climbs gently through meadow, timber and small stream crossings before the ground steepens toward the pass; take the Lake Ann branch to reach the bench and the knoll above it, which has a wide view back down the upper Teanaway. Fortune Peak can also be climbed by its east slope out of Headlight Basin, which is a different camp on the other side of the divide and is described with the Ingalls group rather than here. Mountain goats work this whole area and are bold about salt — keep gear packed and relieve yourself well away from camp.
bivy.water: The bench camp has running water beside it, fed by snowmelt draining the basin, and small streams cross the main basin trail lower down. All of it is snowmelt and all of it fades: reliable through July, marginal in August, and effectively gone by September, when the basin is dry rock and cured grass. There is no water at all on the pass or on either summit.
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness above the basin, under the Cle Elum district and entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area — a free self-issued slip from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, with no quota, no lottery and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the Esmeralda Basin trailhead. No campfires; this is open subalpine meadow and the ban is both seasonal and permanent by elevation. Camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake, which is a different basin over the divide, and the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option on that side.
bivy.capacity: Small scattered sites rather than a campground — a bench part way up the Lake Ann branch takes a tent or two, and a knoll on its east side holds several more; nothing here suits a large group

backups.overview: Bryant Peak (5,801 ft) sits on the ridge between Chair Peak and The Tooth above the Source Lake and Snow Lake basins in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, about 0.65 miles southeast of Chair Peak. Originally named Hemlock Peak, it was renamed in 1925 for Sidney V. Bryant; the peak was first climbed in 1926. It's a popular, moderate scramble often paired with Chair Peak and/or The Tooth on the Alpental skyline traverse. The standard summer line comes up the southwest side from Hemlock Pass, reached by the Denny Creek trail, and is often paired with nearby Hemlock Peak.
backups.beta: From Hemlock Pass the route follows the ridgeline toward Bryant Peak, angling right behind trees to a brushy notch, then climbs roughly 170 ft to a meadow at the base of a talus slope that covers about three-quarters of the peak's base. The final scramble goes up rock on the left (or, when snow-free, around the exposed north side) to the summit; the rock is loose and helmets are recommended.
backups.turnaround: Turn around with enough daylight and margin to reverse the loose, exposed summit scramble before deteriorating weather, wet rock, or fatigue increase fall and rockfall risk.
backups.comms: No confirmed cell coverage data found for this specific route; the broader Snoqualmie Pass/I-90 corridor has patchy but sometimes usable cell signal on ridges and summits, unreliable in valleys and basins.

backups.best_season: Late July through September — the gully and upper slopes often hold snow into July. A separate, more technical winter/early-season ascent (ice axe and crampons required, significant avalanche hazard) is popular but distinct from the summer scramble.
backups.approach: From I-90 Exit 47, take Denny Creek Road (FR 58) about 3 miles, past Denny Creek Campground, then turn left onto FR 5830 to the Denny Creek trailhead (~2,300 ft). Follow the Denny Creek Trail (#1014, the Melakwa Lake trail) up the valley past waterfalls, then up steeper switchbacks to Hemlock Pass, about 4 miles and roughly 2,300 ft above the car. At the crest of the pass turn right and follow the ridge on a bearing of about 33°, skirting cliff bands mainly on the left, to a plateau and meadow on the ridge. Early in the season, while snow still covers the brush, a brushy notch behind trees on the right leads about 170 ft up and then northeast to a meadow at the foot of the talus field that wraps about three-quarters of the peak's base; later in the season that line is choked with brush, so stay on the ridge and go straight up it to the summit block. The final scramble is loose rock on the left, or when snow-free around the exposed north side; helmets are recommended. The round trip is about 9 miles with roughly 3,600 ft of gain for Bryant alone; adding nearby Hemlock Peak makes it about 9.5 miles and 3,900 ft.
backups.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble with no rappels and no fixed anchors. Reverse the ascent: downclimb the loose Class 3 summit block carefully, facing in where it is steep, then return across the talus and down the ridge to Hemlock Pass, keeping to the ascent line around the cliff bands rather than cutting down the fall line. From the pass, follow the Denny Creek Trail back down to the trailhead. The steep gully between Bryant and Chair Peak on the Source Lake side is a separate line and an avalanche path in winter and spring; it is not a descent from this route.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward on this route: reverse course down the talus to Hemlock Pass and the Denny Creek Trail at essentially any point below the final summit rock step.

itinerary.cal: Best late June through September once the Denny Creek Trail and upper snowfields have melted out; earlier-season ascents involve more snow travel and require an ice axe.

approach_variants.baseFinding: HEMLOCK PASS IS WHERE THE TRAIL STOPS CLIMBING. At its crest, before the trail drops toward Melakwa Lake, turn right onto the ridge and hold a bearing of about 33°, skirting the cliff bands mainly on their left. The check that you are on line is a plateau and meadow on the ridge, then a talus field wrapping most of the peak's base with the summit block above. Negative marker: if you are descending toward a lake, you stayed on the trail past the pass.

approach_variants.name: Alpental, Source Lake and Great Scott Basin to the Bryant-Chair gully
approach_variants.notes: A steeper alternative from the Alpental side, better known as a winter and spring snow climb than as a summer scramble. From the Alpental day-use trailhead at about 3,120 ft, take the Snow Lake Trail #1013 through old avalanche brush and second growth. At roughly 1.8 miles and 720 ft of gain, a boot path splits LEFT (southwest) toward Source Lake while the main trail continues right toward Snow Lake Col. Drop briefly to cross Source Lake's outlet creek — the last dependable water — and follow the use trail along the lake's north and east shore into the open basin below The Tooth and Chair Peak. From there the tread becomes intermittent boot-track over boulders and heather benches, climbing southwest into Great Scott Basin under The Tooth's east face. Contour left (south) beneath the broken cliff bands on Bryant's east side and cross a talus field to the foot of the gully.
approach_variants.season: Roughly July to September once the gully has melted out; earlier the gully holds snow and needs an axe and crampons
hazards: The gully is an active avalanche path in winter and spring; avoid it in unstable snow or soon after a storm
Loose scree, with the centre and left of the gully markedly worse than the right
The gully funnels rockfall from parties above
Lingering early-season snow, requiring axe and crampons
Exposed and loose class 3 on the north side of the summit block when the block is dry
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE THUMBTACK IS THE LANDMARK YOU WALK PAST, AND THE GULLY IS THE ONE IMMEDIATELY BEYOND IT. Contouring south beneath Bryant's east side you cross a talus field below the rock spire known locally as the Thumbtack. The mouth of the route's gully is at the far side of that talus. Spire behind you, steep scree-and-talus gully splitting the face in front of you.

WHAT THE GULLY IS, IN OTHER WORDS: this is the same drainage backcountry skiers call the Bryant Couloir or the wonder gully. If your winter partner knows the ski line, they know the route.

THE FOOTING TEST TELLS YOU WHERE TO BE WITHIN IT: climb favouring the FAR CLIMBERS' RIGHT side of the gully, which is noticeably firmer than the loose centre and left. A party grinding up loose ground in the middle is in the correct gully and in the wrong part of it.

WHERE IT DELIVERS YOU: the gully tops out on the BRYANT-CHAIR CONNECTING RIDGE, not on a summit. From there you work SOUTH over blocky ridge and talus to the base of the summit block. A gully that finishes on a summit is not this one.

AND THE LAST STEP CHANGES CHARACTER WITH THE SNOW, which is worth knowing before you commit: with snow on the block the final scramble is easy class 3 with little real exposure. Dry, the only reasonable line goes round the NORTH — climbers' left — side on exposed and distinctly loose class 3. Test every hold.

Early in the season a brushy notch behind trees on the right leads about 170 ft up and then northeast to a meadow; once the snow is gone that notch is choked with brush, so stay on the ridge.

backups.overview: Iron Cap Mountain (6,347 ft) rises above the Williams Lake and La Bohn Gap country near the heart of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness. Despite its modest elevation, it has striking local relief, climbing about 2,500 feet above the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Valley in less than a mile. The mountain straddles two drainages: its south side sheds into tributaries of the Snoqualmie River via the Williams Lake basin, while the north side drains toward the Foss River. It was first climbed in 1925 by a party led by Seattle mountaineer Joe Hazard. This route comes in from the north on the West Fork Foss River trail off US 2, past Trout, Copper and Big Heart lakes to a camp at Chetwoot Lake, and finishes on Iron Cap's west and north ridges.
backups.beta: A long backcountry approach (6.6+ trail miles, ~3,400 ft gain to Chetwoot Lake) followed by off-trail cross-country travel and unroped class 3 scrambling on the west and north ridges. Solid granite in places but loose talus and scree lower down; most parties treat it as a 2-3 day trip with a camp at Big Heart or Chetwoot Lake.
backups.turnaround: Given the long approach and off-trail, unmarked ridge terrain, set a firm turnaround time before setting out and stick to it — losing daylight or getting caught by weather on the loose, exposed class 3 ridge or during cross-country travel back to the trail is the main risk on this route.

Water is plentiful at the lakes along the approach but scarce on the ridge above Chetwoot and Iron Cap lakes; fill up before the climb

backups.pro_needs: No technical protection is needed — this is an unroped class 3 scramble on talus and blocky rock; a helmet is a reasonable precaution against rockfall on the ridge.
backups.approach: Start at the West Fork Foss River trailhead (~1,650 ft): from US 2 at Skykomish, turn south on Foss River Road (FR 68), then left on FR 6835 (signed for Trail 1064) for its last 1.9 miles to the trailhead. Self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permits are at the trailhead. The West Fork Foss Lakes Trail #1064 reaches Trout Lake at 1.6 miles, then climbs to Copper Lake (4.2 miles, about 2,400 ft of gain) and continues past Little Heart Lake to Big Heart Lake (7.3 miles, about 3,300 ft), where the maintained trail ends. From Big Heart, go cross-country over the south end of Atrium Ridge, past small tarns and Little Chetwoot Lake, to Chetwoot Lake, the usual camp. From Chetwoot, climb talus and heather toward Point 6077, pass it on the east through more talus, and gain Iron Cap's west ridge for easy Class 3 scrambling. A short third-class downclimb drops into a notch; beyond it a wide ramp traverses below the summit block, without sidehilling, to the broad north ridge, and easy red-tinged rock and dirt lead to the 6,347 ft summit. A variation climbs from the Iron Cap Lake outlet on ledges around the nose of the north ridge. Route-finding through the boulder fields is the crux of the approach: cairns are sparse, and a map or GPS track is strongly advised. Most parties take two to three days, about 24 miles round trip.
backups.descent_text: Descent reverses the ascent or loops through the Iron Cap Lake basin. From the summit, follow the broad north ridge down on easy red-tinged rock and dirt, then either return across the ramp and up out of the notch onto the west ridge and down the talus to Chetwoot Lake, or continue down the north ridge to Iron Cap Lake and work back to camp through the lake basin. This is a Class 2-3 walk-off with no fixed anchors or rappels. The main hazards are loose dirt over rock, especially when wet or with snow patches early in the season, and picking the wrong line: parties who lose the ramp or wander east end up cliffed out on the steeper east-side rock bands or in steep heather, so retrace your ascent track. From Chetwoot, reverse the cross-country leg over Atrium Ridge to Big Heart Lake and walk the West Fork Foss trail about 7.3 miles back to the trailhead.
backups.bail: Retreat is straightforward at nearly any point on the ridge or the cross-country approach by simply reversing the ascent line back to Chetwoot Lake and the maintained trail — no fixed rappels or technical retreat gear are needed.

itinerary.cal: The lake basins and the ridge typically aren't snow-free until mid-to-late July, so August-September is the most reliable window.

The trail miles are steady; the off-trail leg is slow.

itinerary.totalNote: A 3-day backpack of about 24 miles round trip: a trail day to Big Heart Lake and cross-country to Chetwoot Lake, a summit day of about five hours from camp, and a day out. Strong parties sometimes do it in two days.

access.fees: A Northwest Forest Pass ($5/day or $30/annual) or America the Beautiful pass is required to park at the West Fork Foss trailhead.
access.rules: No motorized or mechanized travel within the Alpine Lakes Wilderness; groups larger than 12 must split into separate parties with at least one mile of separation.
access.permit: Free self-issue day-use/overnight wilderness permit required at the trailhead for all of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness; group size is capped at 12 (people and stock combined).
access.land_manager: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Skykomish Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful pass required at developed trailheads.

overnight_permit.what: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit
overnight_permit.where: Fill one out at the trailhead kiosk and carry your copy.

road.name: Foss River Road (FR 68) and FR 6835
road.status: Gravel forest roads; check Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF road alerts before driving
road.driveNote: From US 2 at Skykomish, turn south on Foss River Road (FR 68), then left on FR 6835 (signed for Trail 1064) for its last 1.9 miles to the West Fork Foss trailhead.

climate.typical: Wet, cool west-slope Cascades climate; heavy winter snowpack persists into early summer, especially on north-facing terrain. Reliable snow-free scrambling conditions typically arrive by late July/August and hold through September.

bySeason.fall: Late September into October: shorter days and rising storm risk; snow can return to the high basin by mid-October.
bySeason.spring: Not viable — approach trail and route are largely snow-covered with high avalanche hazard on surrounding slopes during May-June snowmelt.
bySeason.summer: Best window (August-September): warm, mostly snow-free ridge, though the boulder-field approach still demands care and route-finding.
bySeason.winter: FR 56 and the trail are typically snow-covered and effectively inaccessible; not a winter objective.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass / Stevens Pass zones (the peak sits near the boundary) — check both for early- and late-season travel

emergency.notes: No cell coverage in the West Fork Foss valley or the lake basins below Iron Cap; the approach is remote, so plan for a long hike and drive to reach help in an emergency.
emergency.rangerStation: Skykomish Ranger District, Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (on US 2 at Skykomish; administers the West Fork Foss trailhead)
emergency.nearestHospital: EvergreenHealth Monroe, Monroe (24-hour emergency department), west on US 2

crowds.peakTraffic: Late July-August weekends, mostly parties doing the Alpine Lakes High Route traverse rather than a dedicated Iron Cap day trip
crowds.estimatePerSeason: roughly 20-40 parties per season (rough estimate from trip-report frequency, not a measured count)

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong, sustained uphill fitness: about 7.3 trail miles and 3,300 ft to Big Heart Lake, then slow cross-country travel to Chetwoot Lake before any scrambling begins
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Most parties camp at Chetwoot Lake given the approach length, so plan for an overnight pack (roughly 20-35 lbs) rather than a single big day

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long: a full day on the West Fork Foss trail and over Atrium Ridge to Chetwoot Lake before the climb itself
requiredSkills: Class 3 scrambling on loose talus and short rock steps
off-trail routefinding (route is not signed/maintained)
comfort with loose/exposed footing
self-sufficiency on a long approach far from help
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Advanced scrambler comfortable with sustained off-trail travel and unmaintained wilderness approaches; not a beginner objective

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: August is the core window; late July into September is climbable but with more variable snow/weather at the margins (August) and season (Late July-September)

July.reason: Only the back half of July is in season; early/mid-July can still have lingering snowpack on the approach and route from spring snow cover

August.reason: In season; maritime climate is clearest and driest in mid-to-late summer, giving the most reliable dry-rock talus/scramble conditions

September.reason: Still within the dry summer window, but shorter days and a rising chance of early-season storms as fall approaches (a 'short clear window' in fall)

weather.typical: Maritime Cascades climate; the route window is the driest and clearest in mid-to-late summer, with full snow cover in winter and lingering snow/avalanche risk in spring
weather.probability: Afternoon convective showers are a general Cascades summer pattern; no route-specific thunderstorm frequency data was found for Iron Cap

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Class 3 terrain on loose talus and short rock steps (on-file hazard: loose rock); parties describe a short 3rd-class downclimb near a notch adding fall exposure, and the long, unmaintained approach (on-file hazard: long approach) increases the consequence of any injury given distance from help

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer route (nearest NWAC coverage is the Stevens Pass zone, but Iron Cap is climbed only in the snow-free season, outside the winter/spring avalanche forecast period)

gaps: No official gain_ft/dist_km figures specific to an Iron Cap-only round trip were found; the ~15-mile-to-Williams-Lake and ~30-mile-round-trip figures are derived from trip-report mileages for multi-peak traverses, not a dedicated FS trail log for this exact route

approach_variants.name: Iron Cap Lake basin to the north ridge
approach_variants.notes: However you reach it, the last of the walking is cross-country over open talus, heather benches and scree above the lake basin. Route-finding is the crux of the approach rather than any move on it: the ground is unmarked and lightly cairned, the footing is loose rock and dirt with occasional steep heather, and visibility-dependent cliff bands will stop a poorly chosen line. Water is scarce once you leave the valley floor, so tank up before the final push.
hazards: Loose dirt over rock on the upper slopes
Steep heather with poor runout
Cliff bands on the east side that will stop a badly chosen line
Snow lingering into early July on north-facing ground
No water above the basin
approach_variants.baseFinding: The scrambling begins on rock ledges above the outlet of Iron Cap Lake. Cross the outlet stream and start working upward to the SOUTHEAST on a series of ledges — the change from vegetated, dirt-over-rock ground to continuous clean ledges is the tell that you are on the route, and the rock here is genuinely solid, unlike everything below it. The line curves around the nose of the north ridge rather than attacking the summit block head-on. Higher, a short third-class downclimb drops into a notch, which reads as a dead end and is not one: beyond it a wide ramp traverses below the summit block, taking you across without sidehilling, and meets the broad north ridge. From there easy red-tinged rock and dirt lead to the true summit. Losing that ramp is the way parties end up cliffed out on the steeper east-side rock bands, so note the line as you go and retrace it exactly on the way down.

climbing_route.label: West ridge
climbing_route.notes: Gained off unmarked cross-country ground above Iron Cap Lake basin; loose rock and dirt underfoot with occasional steep heather. Class 2-3 scrambling toward the 6,347 ft summit.

climbing_route.label: Downclimb into the notch
climbing_route.notes: From the ridge a short 3rd-class downclimb drops into a notch.

climbing_route.label: Ramp below the summit block to the north ridge
climbing_route.notes: Beyond the notch a wide ramp traverses below the summit block — no sidehilling required — to meet the broad north ridge, which is easy red-rock and dirt scrambling to the true summit.

bivy.name: Chetwoot Lake
bivy.notes: The base for the climb: reached off-trail from Big Heart Lake over the south end of Atrium Ridge, past small tarns and Little Chetwoot Lake. Much quieter than Big Heart. The climb to Iron Cap's west ridge starts from here.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the West Fork Foss trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve.

bivy.name: Big Heart Lake
bivy.notes: The end of the maintained West Fork Foss trail, about 7.3 miles and 3,300 ft from the trailhead; popular and often crowded, but a reasonable first-night stop for slower parties.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve.
